title: Solidarity
hook: in Poland, striking workers kneel for Mass at the shipyard gate, and faith and a trade union help bring peaceful change

segments.voice: Yesterday, Janani Luwum, an archbishop who signed the letter and raised the killings with the president face to face. Your line was courage in kampala. What true thing did you finally say? Day nine hundred sixty-nine.

The gate of a shipyard in Gdańsk, on the Polish coast, is covered in flowers. Someone has hung a picture of the pope on it, and a wooden cross. Inside, the workers are on strike. Outside, a priest sets up an altar, and the strikers kneel on the concrete for Mass. Others line up for confession on folding chairs by the fence. The government is communist, wary of the church, and it is watching. The workers want a union of their own, free of the party. Today, the word they painted on their banners.

The union was called Solidarność, Solidarity, and an electrician named Lech Wałęsa became its face. It was a trade union, not a church, and its members included believers and nonbelievers. But in Poland, the Catholic Church was a large institution the state didn't control, and the two leaned on each other. The pope was Polish: John Paul the Second. At the start of his time as pope, he told the crowds, in effect, do not be afraid. It is a line Jesus says in the Gospels. When the disciples see him walking on the water, terrified, the King James Bible has him say: "Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid." Before the strikes, when he came home to Poland, crowds gathered in the open for his Masses. Then the crackdown came. Martial law. Solidarity banned. Leaders jailed. In Warsaw a young priest, Jerzy Popiełuszko, said Masses for the homeland, packed with workers, and kept repeating a line from Paul's letter to the Romans: "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good." Secret police officers abducted and killed him. His grave became a place of pilgrimage. And still the movement did not turn to violence. Years later, the government sat down at a round table with Solidarity and agreed to partly free elections, and Solidarity won almost every seat it was allowed to contest. Solidarity is also a word in Christian teaching: the idea that people are bound up with one another, so another's burden is partly yours. Paul says it plainly: "Bear ye one another's burdens."

Here's the practice: hold the people whose work your day rests on. Settle, and breathe. Start with what's around you: the chair, the light, the clothes you're wearing, the food you'll eat later. Somebody built, wired, sewed, grew, drove and cleaned for each of them. Picture a few of those workers. A night shift. A warehouse. A field. A shipyard. Let one of their burdens sit with you for a moment. If you pray, you can pray for workers by name or by trade. If you don't, let the thanks be enough. The bell holds the time.
Solidarity. The Polish trade union that grew alongside the church and helped bring peaceful change. And an old idea: your neighbor's burden is partly yours.
Your line: be not afraid. Today, when fear starts to make a decision for you, stop and ask what you'd do if it didn't. Day nine hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: In Catholic teaching, solidarity is one of the principles of social teaching, and Catholics pray for workers on the feast of Saint Joseph the Worker. Catholics honor Jerzy Popiełuszko as a martyr, and his grave in Warsaw is visited by pilgrims.

notes: Claims rule: no dates or counts in the voice; 'thousands of workers' and 'huge crowds' are the only size words; cut if needed.

'The one large institution the state didn't control': confirm or soften.
Popiełuszko: monthly Masses for the homeland in Warsaw, his use of Romans 12:21, abduction and murder by security service officers, grave as pilgrimage site; beatified as a martyr. Confirm.
